nameStory: The 'slickseed' part of this plant's name comes from its smooth, hairless seeds - quite different from its fuzzy leaves and stems! The scientific name 'leiosperma' means exactly that: 'leios' for smooth and 'sperma' for seed. It's called a 'fuzzybean' because it's covered in soft, silky hairs and produces bean-like pods as a member of the legume family.
description: Slickseed fuzzybean is a delicate, climbing vine that's quite rare in New England, with only three recorded sightings in the region. This diminutive plant produces small, pea-shaped flowers and bean-like pods, all covered in a soft coating of silky hairs. As an annual or short-lived perennial, it's much smaller and more delicate than its fuzzybean relatives. The vine climbs and trails through other vegetation, rarely drawing attention to itself.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feel the soft, silky hairs covering thin leaflets that are rarely lobed - they're noticeably smaller and more delicate than other fuzzybeans

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pea-shaped flowers with wing petals that hide most of the keel - much smaller than other wildbean flowers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Smooth seeds that lack the waxy, hairy coating found on related species - they feel slick to the touch

idTips.label: Pods
idTips.description: Small bean pods covered in the same silky hairs as the leaves and stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A climbing or trailing vine that's noticeably smaller and more delicate overall than its fuzzybean relatives

habitat: In its native range, slickseed fuzzybean prefers drier sites than its relatives, often growing in sandy soils and open areas. Given its extreme rarity in New England with only three observations, it likely occurs as a rare introduction in disturbed soils, field edges, or sandy coastal areas. Look for it climbing through other vegetation in sunny, well-drained locations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin their climbing growth, developing the characteristic silky-haired leaves.
seasonality.summer: Produces its tiny pea-shaped flowers and begins forming the small, fuzzy seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Pods mature and release the distinctive smooth seeds before the plant dies back.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only seeds to survive until the following growing season.

funFact: This tiny vine is one of the few legumes that can pollinate itself - while most beans and peas need insects or other plants to reproduce, slickseed fuzzybean has evolved the ability to be its own matchmaker, which might help explain how it occasionally shows up in unexpected places like New England!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with trailing fuzzy-bean, but slickseed fuzzybean is noticeably smaller in all its parts and has much thinner, rarely lobed leaflets. Remember: if it looks delicate and diminutive with thin leaves, it's probably slickseed; if it's more robust, it's likely trailing fuzzy-bean.
contextualKnowledge: This species is far outside its normal range in New England - it's naturally a plant of the central and western United States. The few New England sightings are likely accidental introductions, making any encounter with this plant particularly noteworthy for botanists and naturalists.
compareHints: Slickseed fuzzybean is the smallest and most delicate of the fuzzybean species, with thinner leaflets that are rarely lobed compared to trailing fuzzy-bean's more robust, often deeply lobed leaves. The key difference is in the seeds - slickseed fuzzybean lives up to its name with smooth seeds, while trailing fuzzy-bean has waxy, hairy seeds. It also tends to grow in drier conditions than its moisture-loving relative.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Trailing fuzzy-bean differs from its relative slickseed fuzzybean primarily in its consistently hairy pods - slickseed fuzzybean has smooth pods as its name suggests.
